blocks.text: Every single thing that happens over an MCP connection, discovering tools, calling one, reading a resource, all of it happens through messages. This lesson looks at the message concept itself, the basic unit everything else in this curriculum, requests, responses, notifications, is ultimately built from, before the Communication Protocol module goes into the exact wire format in full technical depth.
1. A Message Is the Basic Unit of MCP Communication

blocks.alt: A client sends a message to a server

blocks.text: Whatever happens between a client and a server, it happens as one or more messages passed back and forth, a message is simply a piece of structured data following an agreed format, JSON-RPC, that either side can send and the other can reliably interpret.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.content: Think of a message as a single, self-contained envelope, everything needed to understand and act on it is inside that one envelope, nothing is implied from outside context.

blocks.text: This uniform envelope shape is exactly what allows generic client and server libraries to exist at all, the low-level machinery for sending and parsing messages never needs to know what a specific method actually does.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you can describe any MCP interaction as one or more of these three envelope shapes passed back and forth, you understand the foundation the rest of the protocol builds on.

blocks.text: Nothing about a message assumes anything about who sent it or why, that context lives in the surrounding session and application logic, not in the message envelope itself.
2. Three Kinds of Messages

blocks.alt: Request, response, and notification are the three kinds of messages

blocks.text: There are exactly three kinds of messages in MCP, a request, which expects a reply, a response, which is that reply, matched back to its original request, and a notification, a one-way message that expects no reply at all. Every single interaction in MCP is built from these three shapes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Message type","Expects a reply","Example"],"rows":[["Request","Yes","tools/call"],["Response","Is the reply","The result of a tools/call"],["Notification","No","A resource changed"]]}

blocks.text: Almost every operation covered elsewhere in this curriculum, tools/list, tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get, is really just a specific request-and-response pair using this same underlying shape.

Even a seemingly simple interaction, checking the weather, is really a request followed by a response under the hood, the three-message vocabulary applies uniformly no matter how simple or complex the operation looks from the outside.
3. What Every Message Shares

Every message, regardless of type, is a JSON object marked with a jsonrpc field identifying the format version being used, this shared marker is what lets both sides confirm they are speaking the same basic language before even looking at the specific content of the message.

code.content:
# every message includes this same version marker
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", ...}

blocks.text: Two sides using slightly different jsonrpc version numbers would immediately have a compatibility problem, which is exactly why this field is checked early and strictly.
If the jsonrpc field is ever missing or set to an unrecognized value, a well-behaved implementation should reject the message outright rather than attempt to guess its meaning.
4. Requests Carry an id

blocks.alt: A request carries an id field

blocks.text: A request always includes an id, a value the sender chooses, that the eventual response will echo back exactly, this is what allows a client to correctly match an incoming response to whichever specific request it originally corresponds to, even if several requests are in flight at once.
The id can be a number or a string, the specific choice does not matter, what matters is that it is unique enough, within the current session, to avoid ambiguity.

blocks.title: A common convention
blocks.content: Many client implementations simply use an incrementing counter starting from one, guaranteeing uniqueness within a session without any extra coordination.

blocks.text: 5. Responses Echo the Same id Back

blocks.alt: A request with id 5 gets a response with the same id 5

blocks.text: A response always carries the same id as the request it is answering, along with either a result, on success, or an error, on failure, never both at the same time.

code.content:
# a response never contains both result and error at once
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "error": {"code": "invalid_arguments", "message": "city is required"}}

blocks.title: Why never both at once
blocks.content: Allowing both result and error at the same time would leave a client uncertain about which one to actually trust, keeping them mutually exclusive removes that ambiguity entirely.

blocks.text: 6. Notifications Have No id at All

blocks.alt: A notification has no id field

blocks.text: A notification deliberately omits the id field entirely, since there is no reply expected, there is nothing to match a response back to, a server sending a resource-changed notification, for instance, is not asking for anything back, just informing the client something happened.
This is a deliberate, structural signal, not an oversight, seeing a message with no id immediately tells a client it should not wait for, or expect, anything further tied to it.

A server sending a notification has no way of knowing, or needing to know, whether the client actually acted on it, that lack of acknowledgment is an accepted tradeoff for the simplicity of a fire-and-forget message.

blocks.text: 7. Why This Three-Way Split Matters

Keeping requests, responses, and notifications structurally distinct lets both sides handle each one appropriately without ambiguity, a client always knows a message with an id needs a matching reply or is itself that reply, and a message without one never does.
Without this split, a client would have no reliable way to tell whether an incoming message needed a reply from it, was itself a reply, or was simply informational.

This clarity also simplifies writing generic client code, a single dispatch function can look at whether a message has an id and a result or error field, and route it correctly without any special-casing per method.
This same clarity extends to logging and monitoring tools built on top of MCP, which can reliably tally requests, responses, and notifications separately without needing custom logic per method.
It also simplifies error handling for the whole system, since a failure only ever needs to be represented inside a response, never as some ambiguous fourth message type.
8. Every Higher-Level Operation Is Built From These

Listing tools, calling a tool, reading a resource, filling in a prompt, every single one of these is, underneath, just a request message followed by a matching response message, the specific method name and params differ, the underlying message shape does not.

code.content:
# tools/call is just a specific request method name and params shape
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 9, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {}}}

blocks.content: {"headers":["Higher-level operation","Underlying method name"],"rows":[["Listing tools","tools/list"],["Calling a tool","tools/call"],["Reading a resource","resources/read"]]}

blocks.text: Recognizing this pattern early makes every future lesson about a specific MCP method easier to absorb, since the underlying mechanics never actually change, only the method name and the shape of params and result.
9. Messages Travel Over a Transport

blocks.alt: A message travels over a transport to its destination

blocks.text: A message itself does not care whether it travels over standard input and output for a local process or over an HTTP connection for a remote one, the transport, covered in its own dedicated module, is simply the pipe the message travels through, the message format stays identical either way.
This separation of message format from transport is exactly what lets the same client code work whether it happens to be talking to a local stdio server or a remote HTTP based one.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If you ever find yourself debugging a transport issue, framing, encoding, connection drops, remind yourself that the message content itself is a completely separate concern.

code.content:
# the exact same message, sent over two different transports
# stdio: written as one line of JSON to stdout
# http: sent as the body of a POST request

blocks.text: 10. Ordering and Concurrency

Multiple requests can be in flight at the same time, their responses do not necessarily need to arrive in the same order they were sent, this is exactly why the id field matters so much, it is the only reliable way to match a response to its request when things do not arrive in a strict sequence.

blocks.title: A practical implication
blocks.content: A client sending several requests in parallel needs to be prepared for their responses to come back in any order, and must rely on id matching rather than arrival order.

blocks.text: A client that assumes strict ordering, matching responses purely by arrival sequence instead of by id, will eventually mismatch a response to the wrong request under load.
A well-designed client stores pending requests in a lookup keyed by id specifically to handle this, resolving each one the moment its matching response arrives, regardless of order.
11. Batching Several Messages Together

blocks.alt: Message 1 and message 2 get batched together

blocks.text: Some implementations allow several messages to be sent together in a single batch, reducing round trips, this is covered fully in the Batching lesson in the Communication Protocol module, for now it is enough to know a single transport send does not always carry exactly one message.
Not every client or server implementation supports batching, it is an optional capability rather than a universal requirement of the protocol.
Even where supported, batching is usually an optimization applied selectively, most day-to-day traffic is still simple, one message at a time.
12. Debugging by Reading Raw Messages

When something goes wrong in an MCP-based system, looking at the actual raw messages exchanged, often with a tool like the MCP Inspector covered later in this curriculum, is one of the fastest ways to see exactly where a request failed to get the expected response.
Even without specialized tooling, simply logging every outgoing and incoming message during development is often enough to spot a mismatched id or an unexpectedly shaped response.
Building this habit early, checking raw messages before assuming a bug is somewhere more complicated, saves significant debugging time once real MCP servers and clients are involved.
13. A Worked Example
Trace three messages in sequence, a request, its response, and an unrelated notification arriving afterward.
Notice the notification at the end carries no id and expects nothing back, the client can choose to act on it, refreshing its resource list, without ever needing to send a reply.

code.content:
# a client dispatch function using the type-detection logic from earlier
def classify(msg):
    if "id" not in msg: return "notification"
    return "response" if "result" in msg or "error" in msg else "request"

blocks.text: Try extending this trace by adding a second, concurrent request with a different id, and confirming its response can arrive before or after the first one without causing any confusion.
14. Common Mistakes When Thinking About Messages

items: Assuming every message expects a reply, notifications explicitly do not.
Forgetting to match a response back to its request by id, especially when multiple requests are in flight concurrently.
Confusing the message format, JSON-RPC, with the transport carrying it, they are two entirely separate layers.
Assuming responses always arrive in the same order requests were sent, this is not guaranteed.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is trying to reuse the same id for two different in-flight requests, breaking the client’s ability to match responses correctly.
An eighth common mistake is writing client code that blocks forever waiting for a response to something that was actually sent as a notification, since no response is ever coming.
15. Practice: Classify Some Messages

Look at three example JSON messages and classify each one as a request, a response, or a notification, based solely on whether it has an id and whether it is a result or error versus a fresh method call.

code.content:
messages = [
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"tools": []}},
    {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/tools/list_changed"},
]
for m in messages:
    kind = "notification" if "id" not in m else ("response" if "result" in m or "error" in m else "request")
    print(kind)

blocks.text: Once you can classify these three confidently, try writing out, by hand, what the notification and request messages would look like for a made-up new method of your choosing.
A useful final check is writing the exact response message that would answer each request in your practice set, reinforcing how the id field ties the two together.
Key Takeaway

A message is the basic unit of everything that happens in MCP, coming in exactly three shapes, requests that expect a reply, responses that are that reply matched by id, and notifications that expect nothing back at all, every higher-level MCP operation is ultimately built from just these three simple shapes.
This lesson sets up the vocabulary the next two lessons dig into individually, Requests first, then Responses, each covered in far more depth than the brief overview given here.

The batching concept from the newly added section is a small but practical detail worth remembering once you reach the Communication Protocol module, since it changes how a client needs to read incoming data off the transport.
